title: Scripture for Someone Who Is Grieving
h1: Scripture for someone who is grieving
kicker: For the weeks after the funeral
description: A free printable sheet of Scripture for the days and weeks after a loss, with what to say and what not to say. For friends, pastors, hospice workers, and anyone who wants to show up well.
moment: The funeral is over, the casseroles have stopped, and the house is quiet for the first time. This is the stretch nobody prepares you for, and the stretch where a friend who shows up matters most. These passages are for then. Pick one. Read it slowly. You don’t need to explain it.

refs.why: Near to the brokenhearted. It asks nothing of the person but being broken, which is where they are.
Jesus wept at a tomb he was about to empty. Grief is not a failure of faith; it is the right response to loss.
Blessed are those who mourn. Jesus doesn’t tell them to stop, and he doesn’t say when the comfort comes.
New every morning, written in a burned city. Not a promise the day will be good; a promise you weren’t abandoned in the night.
Weeping may stay for the night. The night can be long. Someone who has been through one says it ends.

sections.h: For later, when they are ready

refs.why: The God of all comfort, from a man who needed comforting and got it. Eventually, their grief will be what someone else needs. Not yet.
Every tear wiped away. Offer it once, quietly, and let them decide when.

say: “I don’t have anything wise to say. I loved her too.”
Say the name. People in grief say the worst part is when everyone stops saying it.
“I’m dropping dinner on the porch Tuesday. No need to answer the door.”
In three weeks, when it’s quietest, send one line: “Thinking of you today. No reason.”
dontSay: “Everything happens for a reason.” Not in the Bible.
“She’s in a better place.” They want her here.
“Let me know if you need anything.” They won’t. Say what you’ll do and when.
use: Choose one passage and keep it for a month rather than reading all seven. If you’re sending one, Psalm 34:18 and one honest sentence is enough. Romans 8:28 is true and it is the wrong verse for fresh grief; save it for the one-year mark.

title: Wedding Scripture by Moment
h1: Wedding Scripture, by moment in the ceremony
kicker: For officiants, couples, and anyone writing the card
description: A free printable guide to wedding Scripture organized by moment in the ceremony: gathering, love and commitment, companionship, blessing, benediction. Where each reading comes from, and four short ones for a card.
moment: Most wedding readings were not written about weddings, and that is fine; the original setting is usually what makes the reading strong. This sheet is arranged by where each passage belongs in a ceremony, with one line on where it comes from, so the couple hears it as it was meant. Tell them in one sentence before the rehearsal. It changes how the room listens.

refs.why: This is the day. The decision to be glad is made before the day proves itself.
“Let us exalt his name together.” For a couple who want the first thing they do married to be worship.
Written to a church that was fighting, as a description of what they were failing to be. It works at a wedding because it defines love as behavior under pressure, not feeling under candlelight.
“Where you go, I will go.” Said by a widowed daughter-in-law to her mother-in-law, not a bride. Still the best statement of chosen loyalty in the Bible; the couple should know who said it.
Love as strong as death, unquenchable by many waters. The Bible’s one book of love poetry, read plainly.
The first wedding, and the line Jesus later quotes: two become one flesh. “It is not good for the man to be alone” is the Bible’s first “not good.”
Two are better than one; a cord of three strands is not quickly broken. Practical and unsentimental.
Compassion, kindness, humility, patience, forgiveness, and above all love. A list a marriage can be measured against on a Tuesday.
The blessing Aaron was told to say over the people, word for word. Nobody has ever minded receiving it.
Humility, gentleness, patience, bearing with one another in love. Written about a church; describes a kitchen just as well.
Sincere love, honoring one another above yourselves, patient in trouble. For the years after the honeymoon.
Do justly, love mercy, walk humbly. Nine words for a life together.
One line, and everyone knows it.
“Let us love one another, for love is of God.” Short and it grounds the marriage in something larger.
Kindness and truth. Write them on your heart. Six words.
The first line of the blessing, if the card is small.

say: Before the rehearsal, tell the couple where each reading comes from, in one sentence.
If the room includes many beliefs, Ecclesiastes 4 and Ruth 1 ask nothing of the listener.
For a second marriage, Isaiah 43:18–19 and Lamentations 3:22–23 acknowledge a past without dwelling on it.
use: Two readings, not four. One about love, one about the long haul. If you use 1 Corinthians 13, say what it is: a rebuke that became the most beautiful description of love ever written. The couple will remember that.

title: Scripture for Waiting on Test Results
h1: Scripture for waiting on test results
kicker: One page for the pocket, the waiting room, and the night before
description: A free one-page printable of Scripture for the wait between the test and the result: five passages for a heart kept steady before the news, and what to say to someone who is waiting.
moment: Nothing to do, no news, every phone call a possible verdict. Waiting is its own kind of hard, and most verses people send are secretly about the news being good. These five are not. They are for the person by the phone, and they were written by people who then got the news, good and bad. Fold this and keep it in a pocket.

refs.why: Though the fig tree doesn’t flourish, yet I will rejoice. The Bible’s clearest trust that doesn’t depend on the news being good. Say it before the call, so it’s already said.
For sleep. Someone else is on watch.
A heart steady before the news, not after it. The only steadiness available while the phone hasn’t rung.
Five promises, and a hand. The verse doesn’t describe the news. It describes the company.

sections.h: Every time the mind runs ahead

refs.why: Tomorrow will worry about itself. Today, the whole assignment is waiting. That is enough.

say: “I know you’re waiting. I’m not going to ask. I’m just here.”
“Whatever it is, you won’t hear it alone. Call me right after.”
Offer to sit with them the night before, or to be there when the call comes.
dontSay: “I’m sure it’s nothing.” You don’t know that, and they know you don’t.
use: Pick one for the night before and one for the morning. Say them out loud. When the mind runs to tomorrow, name today’s one task, which is waiting, and come back to it. It’s a practice, not a switch.

title: What to Read When Someone Is Dying
h1: What to read when someone is dying
kicker: For hospice, the bedside, and the last days
description: A free printable for the bedside: short passages to read aloud to someone who is dying, what to say, and what to leave unsaid. For family, chaplains, hospice staff, and clergy.
moment: At a bedside you need verses that are short, plain, and true, because the person may be drifting and you will be reading through your own tears. These are the ones hospice chaplains reach for. None of them argues. They say: you are held, you are going somewhere, and you are not going alone. Read one, slowly. Then sit. The sitting is most of it.

refs.why: The person has probably known it their whole life, and hearing it now connects the end to everything before. It names the valley and walks through it.
When you pass through the waters, I will be with you. When, not if. Honest about the crossing.
Jesus, dying, to the man dying next to him: today. The shortest, clearest promise in the Bible about what comes next, made to someone with nothing left to offer.
“Into your hand I commend my spirit.” Jesus said it on the cross. If the person can still speak, they may want to say it. If not, say it for them.
A prepared place, and someone coming back to get you. From the one who went first.
Precious in his sight. One line, for when nobody knows what to say.

say: Say less. One verse, slowly. Then hold a hand.
“You can go when you’re ready. We’ll be all right.” Families often need to give permission, and the dying often wait for it.
Say what they meant to you, in the present tense, while they can hear it. Hearing is usually the last sense to go.
Play the music they loved. Read the psalm they knew. Familiar beats profound now.
dontSay: “Fight this.” Late in dying, it becomes one more thing they are failing at.
use: Bring two verses, not seven. Psalm 23 for the room, Luke 23:43 or Psalm 31:5 for the person. If you don’t know what they believed, Psalm 23 and Isaiah 43:2 ask nothing of the listener.

title: Scripture for Caregivers
kicker: For the long haul: aging parents, dementia, cancer, the hospital chair
description: A free printable of Scripture for caregivers: the exhausted spouse, the adult child driving to appointments, the one who sleeps in the hospital chair. Passages about being carried while you carry someone.
moment: Caregiving is love with a schedule, and it goes on longer than anyone plans for. The person you care for gets the visitors and the prayers; you get the pharmacy run. These passages are for you, the one in the chair. They don’t ask you to be stronger. They say who is carrying you while you carry someone else.

refs.why: Come to me, all who labor and are heavily burdened. Then a yoke, which is a tool for work. Not less to carry; a way of carrying it with someone gentle.
He gives power to the weak. The order of the images matters: eagle, then running, then walking without fainting. Most of caregiving is the walking. That, too, is renewed strength.
My flesh and my heart fail. The psalm allows the failing. Something holds underneath it.
Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord. Written to people whose work nobody honored. Yours is seen.
“Inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me.” The pharmacy run counts.

sections.h: When you resent it, and then feel guilty

refs.why: Near to the brokenhearted, and the crushed. Resentment and exhaustion are not failures; they are what crushing feels like. The nearness comes anyway.
Let’s not be weary in doing good. Paul names the weariness first. He doesn’t pretend it away.

say: To yourself: “I can be tired and still be doing this well.”
To a caregiver you know: “What can I take off your plate this week?” Then take it. Not “let me know.”
“Go home and sleep. I’ll sit with her tonight.” The single most useful sentence a friend can say.
dontSay: To a caregiver: “You’re a saint.” It closes the door on them ever admitting it’s hard.
use: Tape one of these to the dashboard or the pill organizer. Psalm 73:26 for the bad days. Matthew 25:40 for the invisible ones. And please, accept the help when it’s offered; letting someone sit with your mother for an evening is not a failure of love.

title: When You Don’t Know What to Say
h1: When you don’t know what to say
kicker: A one-page leave-behind: three passages and three human sentences
description: A free one-page printable for the moment you want to comfort someone and have no words: three passages that ask nothing of them, and three sentences you can actually say.
moment: You want to say something and everything sounds wrong. Good. That instinct is correct; most of what people say in these moments is wrong. Here are three passages that ask nothing of the person, and three sentences that are honest. Say one. Then be quiet.
say: “I don’t have anything wise to say. I just wanted to be here.”
“I’m not going to ask how you are. I’m going to bring dinner Tuesday.”
“I keep thinking about [name].”
use: Pick one passage and one sentence. That is a complete visit.

title: For Tonight, When You Can’t Sleep
h1: For tonight, when you can’t sleep
kicker: A one-page leave-behind: five passages, no commentary
description: A free one-page printable for sleepless nights: five short passages to read at 2 a.m., with no commentary, because at 2 a.m. you don’t want any.
moment: It’s late and your mind won’t stop. You don’t need an explanation right now; you need something short and true to read instead of the ceiling. Five passages. Read one. Read it again. Put the phone down.
use: Keep this on the nightstand. If the nights keep coming, the page for when you can’t sleep has more, and a doctor has more than that.

title: Funeral Scripture by Situation
kicker: For clergy, families, and funeral directors
description: A free printable guide to funeral Scripture organized by situation: sudden death, long illness, a child, an elder, unknown faith, suicide. Every passage in full, with a line on where it fits and where it can hurt.
moment: A funeral is not the place to discover a passage doesn’t fit. These are grouped by the situation you are actually walking into, with a line on why each one works there and where it can go wrong. All text is from the World English Bible and can be copied straight into an order of service.

refs.why: Confident because of the shepherd, not because the road is safe. It names the valley of the shadow of death without flinching, which is why it is read so often.
Jesus, the night before his own death, telling frightened friends there is a prepared place. Read it as a promise from someone who has been through the door.
The last page of the story. Best read near the end of the service, after the grief has been given room, not as a way to skip it.
Paul’s list of everything that cannot separate us from God’s love begins with death. Sturdy, and works for families with mixed beliefs because it makes no demands of the listener.
Nearness to the brokenhearted, promised without conditions. Written by David after a humiliating day, which is why it sounds like it was written from the floor.
Jesus wept at a tomb he was about to empty. Two words that give the whole room permission to grieve without apology.
A psalm for when the earth gives way. It doesn’t say the earth won’t; it says where the refuge is while it does.
Mercy new every morning, written in a burned city. Honest enough for a funeral where nothing makes sense yet.
A course finished and a faith kept. Right for someone who endured well; use with care if the illness stripped the person of the capacity to ‘fight.’
Rest for the heavily burdened. Fits the person who has died and the caregivers who are exhausted in the front row.
The outer person wasting away while the inner is renewed. Paul’s own words about a body giving out, without pretending it isn’t.
‘Precious in Yahweh’s sight is the death of his saints.’ One line, and it says the death was noticed and valued, not merely permitted.
Jesus taking children in his arms and blessing them, over the disciples’ objection. Read it without comment.
David after the death of his infant son: ‘I will go to him, but he will not return to me.’ Grief and hope in one sentence, from a father.
Formed in the womb, every day written before one of them came to be. It says the short life was known and whole.
The shepherd gathering the lambs in his arms and carrying them close. An image, not an argument, which is what the day can bear.
Moses on the length of a life and the wisdom of counting days. Fitting for someone who counted theirs well.
Still bearing fruit in old age, ‘full of sap and green.’ For someone who kept going.
The finished race. Nearly always right for a faithful elder.
‘Even to old age I am he, and even to gray hairs I will carry you.’ A promise kept to the end; read it as fulfilled.

sections.h: When the person’s faith is unknown, or the family’s is

refs.why: A time to be born and a time to die. Recognizable to almost everyone, honest about mortality, and it asks nothing of the hearer.
‘As a father has compassion on his children.’ Frailty and mercy together; the ‘dust’ line is unusually honest for a funeral.
Blessed are those who mourn. A single sentence that dignifies the grief in the room without preaching at it.
Read as a description of God’s disposition rather than a test of the listener’s.
Nearness to the crushed in spirit. The most important verse for this room, and it applies to the person who died as much as to those who remain.
The only psalm that ends in darkness. Reading it says the Bible knows what despair sounds like and kept it in the canon.
Nothing, including death, separates from God’s love. Read it plainly and let it stand.
Elijah asking to die, and God’s answer: food, sleep, and a touch. A gentle passage for a family asking why they didn’t see it.

use: Pick two or three passages, not six. Read them slowly. If a verse needs a paragraph of explanation to fit the situation, choose a different verse. For a graveside committal, Psalm 23 or John 14:1–3 alone is enough.

title: Scripture for the Hospital Room
kicker: For the bedside, the waiting room, and the drive over
description: A free printable of eight passages for the hospital room: before surgery, waiting for news, a long stay, and when there are no words, with what to say when you arrive and when you leave.
moment: Eight passages that hold up at a bedside, and a few words to say with them. Read one. Then stop. Presence matters more than words.

refs.why: Five promises in one verse. The last one is a hand.
The presence goes in with you.
For the night before.
A heart steady before the result.
Each worry turned into a request. The peace stands guard.
For the patient and the family in the chair.
Confident because of the shepherd.
Read it and sit down.

say: Arriving: “I don’t have anything wise to say. I just wanted to be here.”
Offering a verse: “Can I read you something short? You don’t have to say anything back.”
Leaving: “I’ll be back Thursday. You don’t need to remember that; I will.”
